rows.stem: Which one of the following is not used as a vector for rDNA technology ?
rows.solution: A vector is the DNA vehicle that carries a foreign gene into a host and replicates there. **Plasmids**, **bacteriophages** and **retroviruses** (disarmed, in animal cells) are all used as vectors in recombinant DNA technology, because each is a self-replicating piece of DNA (or a virus) that can carry inserted DNA into a cell. A bacterial cell is not a vector: it is the **host** (for example E. coli) into which the recombinant vector is introduced and in which it multiplies. So the answer is option (B) Bacterial cell.

rows.stem: Allergic reactions are countered by the administration of :
rows.solution: An allergy is the exaggerated response of the immune system to certain antigens (allergens). The IgE antibodies produced cause mast cells to release chemicals like **histamine** and serotonin, which bring on the symptoms (sneezing, watery eyes, running nose, difficulty in breathing). These symptoms are quickly reduced by drugs that block or counter histamine, namely **anti-histamines**, together with adrenalin and steroids. Glucagon and insulin regulate blood sugar and oxytocin acts in parturition and milk ejection, so none of them counters an allergy. So the answer is option (C) Antihistamine.

rows.stem: The expected phenotypic ratio amongst the progeny of 60 individuals, obtained from a cross between heterozygous tall pea plant and dwarf pea plant is :
rows.solution:
A heterozygous tall plant (Tt) crossed with a dwarf plant (tt) is a **test cross**:
- Gametes: the tall parent gives T and t in equal numbers; the dwarf parent gives only t.
- Progeny: Tt (tall) and tt (dwarf) in the ratio **1 : 1**.

Out of 60 progeny, half are tall and half are dwarf: 30 tall and 30 dwarf. So the answer is option (C) 30 tall and 30 dwarf.

rows.stem: In the absence of fertilization, corpus luteum :

options.label: D
options.text: produces both oestrogen and progesterone in equal amount

rows.solution: After ovulation the remaining parts of the Graafian follicle form the **corpus luteum**, which secretes large amounts of progesterone to maintain the endometrium for implantation. If fertilisation does not take place, the corpus luteum **degenerates**. Progesterone then falls, the endometrium disintegrates, and menstruation follows, marking a new cycle. So the answer is option (A) degenerates.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : A recombinant DNA which is inserted within the coding sequence of \(\beta\)-galactosidase does not produce blue coloured colonies when treated with a chromogenic substrate.
Reason (R) : Insertional inactivation occurs when a recombinant DNA is introduced in the coding sequence of the enzyme.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is true. In vectors such as pUC, the foreign DNA is inserted within the coding sequence of the enzyme **\(\beta\)-galactosidase**. With no insert, the bacteria carrying the plasmid produce the enzyme and give **blue coloured colonies** in the presence of a chromogenic substrate. When the recombinant DNA is inserted inside the gene, the enzyme is not made, so the colonies are **colourless (white)**.

The Reason is also true and explains it: this inactivation of the enzyme gene by inserting foreign DNA into its coding sequence is called **insertional inactivation**. It is because of insertional inactivation that the recombinant colonies do not turn blue, which lets recombinants be told apart from non-recombinants.

So both statements are true and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion, which is option (A).

rows.stem: How is Ti plasmid of Agrobacterium tumefaciens modified to act as a cloning vector ?
rows.solution:
Agrobacterium tumefaciens, a pathogen of several dicot plants, delivers a piece of its DNA, the **T-DNA** of the **Ti (tumour inducing) plasmid**, into plant cells and transforms them into tumour cells. The Ti plasmid is modified into a cloning vector as follows:
- The **tumour inducing (pathogenic, virulent) genes** of the Ti plasmid are removed, so the plasmid is **disarmed** and no longer pathogenic to the plant.
- The DNA carrying the **gene of interest** is inserted into this segment, so the plasmid can still use its natural mechanism to deliver the desired gene into a variety of plants.

rows.stem:
The first clinical gene therapy was given in 1990 to a 4-year-old girl with ADA deficiency.
(a) Mention the cause of this disorder.
(b) List the possible treatments available for this disorder.
(c) How can this disorder be cured permanently ?
Describe any three assisted reproductive techniques practised to treat infertility.
rows.solution:
[CBSE marking scheme: under GIFT the scheme says the ovum is transferred into the fallopian tube of a female "who can produce one"; NCERT says a female who **cannot** produce an ovum but can provide a suitable environment, which is the whole point of the technique, and that is the reading given here.] Assisted reproductive technologies (ART) treat infertility. Any three of these:
- **In vitro fertilisation followed by embryo transfer (IVF-ET), the "test tube baby" programme**: ova from the wife or a donor and sperms from the husband or a donor are collected and induced to form a zygote under simulated conditions in the laboratory. The zygote or early embryo is then transferred into the female.
- **Zygote intra fallopian transfer (ZIFT)**: the zygote or early embryo with **up to 8 blastomeres** is transferred into the fallopian tube.
- **Intra uterine transfer (IUT)**: embryos with **more than 8 blastomeres** are transferred into the uterus.
- **Gamete intra fallopian transfer (GIFT)**: an ovum collected from a donor is transferred into the fallopian tube of another female who cannot produce one but can provide a suitable environment for fertilisation and further development.
- **Intra cytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI)**: a sperm is injected directly into the ovum to form an embryo in the laboratory.
- **Artificial insemination (AI)**: semen collected from the husband or a healthy donor is artificially introduced into the vagina or the uterus (IUI) of the female, used where the male partner cannot inseminate or has a very low sperm count.

rows.stem:
(a) List the salient features of Darwin's theory of natural selection.
(b) Microbes have proved to be suitable examples to study evolution by natural selection. Justify giving reasons.
rows.solution:
(a) Salient features of Darwin's theory of natural selection:
- Populations have built-in variation and can grow **exponentially**, but resources are limited, so the members of a population **compete for resources**.
- Only some survive and grow; the weaker ones perish. Individuals with **favourable variations** survive and reproduce more, which is the **survival of the fittest**. Fitness ultimately means reproductive fitness: leaving more progeny.
- These favourable variations are **inherited** and get **accumulated** over a period of time, generation after generation.
- The variants are thus **naturally selected**, and over long periods this leads to the origin of **new forms** (species).

(b) Microbes are suitable for studying evolution by natural selection because they **divide very fast** and have a **short life span**, so a very large population passes through many generations in a short time. Changes in the population can therefore be observed within hours or days. For example, bacteria growing on a medium given an antibiotic: those carrying a resistant variation survive and multiply, and soon form most of the population, the same process that would take millions of years in large organisms.

rows.stem:
Answer the following questions that are based on "Hershey and Chase" experiment using E. coli and bacteriophage :
(i) Why did they use radioactive sulphur \(^{35}\text{S}\) and radioactive phosphorus \(^{32}\text{P}\) in their respective culture media for growing E. coli population which subsequently were infected by bacteriophage ?
(ii) State the purpose of their using the following :
(1) Blender
(2) Centrifuge
(iii) Write the observations they made during the course of their experiment.
(iv) Based on the results, write the conclusion they arrived at the end of their experiment.
rows.solution:
(i) Hershey and Chase used radioactive isotopes to tell the two components of the bacteriophage apart:
- **Sulphur** is a component of **protein** but not of DNA, so viruses grown with radioactive sulphur, \(^{35}\text{S}\), had a radioactive **protein coat**.
- **Phosphorus** is a component of **DNA** but not of protein, so viruses grown with radioactive phosphorus, \(^{32}\text{P}\), had radioactive **DNA**.

This let them follow which of the two, protein or DNA, enters the bacterium during infection.

(ii) (1) **Blender**: after the phages were allowed to infect E. coli, the culture was agitated in a blender to **remove the viral coats** from the bacteria.
(2) **Centrifuge**: spinning in a centrifuge **separated the virus particles from the bacteria**, the heavier bacteria settling as a pellet and the lighter viral coats staying in the supernatant.

(iii) Observations:
- With \(^{35}\text{S}\)-labelled (protein-labelled) phages, **no radioactivity was detected in the bacterial cells**; it was found in the **supernatant**, with the protein coats.
- With \(^{32}\text{P}\)-labelled (DNA-labelled) phages, **radioactivity was detected in the bacterial cells** and not in the supernatant.

So the DNA, not the protein, passed from the virus into the bacteria.

(iv) Conclusion: **DNA is the genetic material** that is passed from virus to bacteria, not protein.

rows.stem:
(i) Describe the process of transcription in prokaryotes with respect to initiation, elongation and termination.
(ii) Write how many types of RNA polymerases are used in transcription in
(1) Prokaryotes,
(2) Eukaryotes.
rows.solution:
(i) Transcription in prokaryotes is carried out by a single DNA-dependent RNA polymerase in three steps:
- **Initiation**: the RNA polymerase binds to the **promoter**, which lies at the 3' end of the template strand (upstream of the structural gene), with the help of the initiation factor, **sigma (\(\sigma\))**, and transcription begins.
- **Elongation**: the polymerase uses **nucleoside triphosphates** as substrates and polymerises them in a template-dependent fashion, following the **rule of complementarity**. It also helps to open the helix as it moves along.
- **Termination**: once the polymerase reaches the **terminator** region, the termination factor, **rho (\(\rho\))**, associates with it, and the nascent RNA falls off along with the RNA polymerase, ending transcription.

In bacteria the mRNA needs no processing to become active, and transcription and translation can take place in the same compartment.

(ii) (1) Prokaryotes: **one** type of RNA polymerase (DNA-dependent RNA polymerase) transcribes all the types of RNA.
(2) Eukaryotes: **three** types of RNA polymerase in the nucleus: RNA polymerase I (rRNAs), RNA polymerase II (hnRNA, the precursor of mRNA) and RNA polymerase III (tRNA, 5S rRNA and snRNAs).
